column2: Entering the ancient cave of Brahman, he saw the earth's sacrifice before the Bharata; and he of supreme deeds lifted up the earth, throwing into turmoil daityas, serpents and danavas.
They declare his many foods; they declare that he is the vehicle in battle; the sky, earth and heaven all stand under the control of the eternal one.
He of pot-born seed created the ancient one in whom Vasishtha is said to have been born; he is the Wind, the lord, the horse-swift, the rayed Savita, the first god.
By him all the asuras were conquered; by his prowess the three worlds here were conquered; he is of gods, men and ancestors; they call him the extension of those who know sacrifice.
He alone rises, dividing time; his are the north and south courses; his rays go up, across and down, heating the earth.
Brahmins who know the Veda serve him; the Sun shines using his brightness; he arranges the sacrifice month after month; Veda-knowers recite him at the sacrifice.

He, with one yoke, bears this three-naved wheel drawn by seven horses; of great radiance, all-going, lion of all, Krishna alone upholds the worlds. Eating or not eating, the steadfast; come to Krishna, Partha, the doer always.
Once, the great soul, pervading, satisfied at Khandava, as the smoke-bannered fire, conquered rakshasas and serpents, and everywhere offers all into the fire.
He gave the horse the white horse; he made all the horses; his chariot has three struts and three wheels, with three heads and four corners.
He set the sky in order with five naves; he made the earth, heaven and atmosphere, and likewise created lovely mountains: Hrishikesha of immeasurably blazing fiery splendour.
Crossing rivers, wishing to kill, he drove back that thunderbolt as it struck; as Mahendra he is praised at the great sacrifice by brahmins, alone, with thousands of ancient Rik verses.
Durvasa could be lodged in a house, O king, by him and no other, of great might; they call him the one ancient sage; he, maker of the universe, ordains states of his own self.
He who is the presiding god that makes the Vedas known, and the rules and ancient practices he relies upon, and whatever the fruit in desire, Veda and worldly life: know all this through Vishvaksena.
The white lights in all the world, the three worlds, the three world-guardians, the three fires and the three utterances: all the gods are in Devaki's son.
Year, season, fortnight, day and night, the kalas and kashthas, matras, muhurtas, lavas and kshanas: know all this in Vishvaksena.
Moon and sun, planets, stars, constellations, all new-moon days and full-moon days, the conjunctions of stars and the seasons, Partha: all this is born from Vishvaksena.
Rudras, Adityas, Vasus, the two Ashvins, Sadhyas, Vishvedevas, the six hosts of Maruts, Prajapati, Aditi mother of the gods, and the seven sages: all from Krishna.
Becoming wind, he scatters the universe; becoming fire, he burns, of all forms; becoming water, he submerges all; becoming Brahma, he creates hosts of the universe.
What is to be known and what makes the Vedas known, the rule and what is ordained and relied on: in dharma, Veda and strength, know Keshava as all, moving and unmoving.
That supreme one, in front, became light, illuminating with splendour, of universal form; having created the waters, the self-existent, self-born, he made the whole universe.
Seasons, portents, many marvels, clouds, lightning, all, and Airavata: all moving and unmoving things are from Krishna; know him as Vishnu, called the Universe.
They call Vasudeva the dwelling of the universe, free of qualities; Sankarshana the living being; then Pradyumna, and Aniruddha as the fourth; the self-born great soul commands.
In five ways, joined with the five peoples, urging on, wishing to create this universe, he then made earth, wind, space, light and water, Partha.

Having made this four-fold world, moving and unmoving, he then set the earth with five seeds; heaven will place abundant water on earth; by him this was made, O king; self-born, he gives life by himself.
Then the gods, asuras, men, worlds, sages, ancestors and subjects, briefly, all the various worlds of living beings: the lord of beings, wishing to create always.
Good and bad, moving and unmoving: know all this to be from Vishvaksena. What is and what will be here: know all this as Keshava.
And death for beings at the end is Krishna himself, the eternal bearer of dharma; whatever has been that we do not know here: know all this from Vishvaksena.
Whatever is praised in the worlds, holy, and whatever is good or bad, all that is Keshava; the inconceivable would be otherwise.
Such is this Keshava, self-existent Narayana, supreme and imperishable, the middle of this world and of those that stand, the origin and dissolution of all beings.
[Vasudeva] Listen attentively, O king, best of the Bharatas, as I tell the virtues of brahmins truly, best of the Kurus.
Pradyumna, angered by brahmins, asked: "What fruit is there in worship of brahmins, Madhusudana, for one who is a lord, here and hereafter?
Always honouring the twice-born, what fruit is there, giver of honour? Tell me all this, father; I have a great doubt here."
So addressed by Pradyumna then, I replied to him, great king; hear it attentively.
Know, son of Rukmini, the fruit of worshipping brahmins: they are indeed the kings of soma, the lords of happiness and sorrow.
In this world, son of Rukmini, and in the next, child, happiness has brahmins foremost; I have no doubt here.
Valour, life, fame, glory and strength have brahmins foremost; the worlds and the world-lords are all preceded by brahmins.
So how should I not honour them, child, as if I were a lord? Mighty-armed, let there be no anger in you toward the twice-born.
They could create other worlds and world-lords too; how should I not behave toward them, knowing rightly their great radiance?
A brahmin, tawny, dwelt in my house, my son, clad in rags, bearing a bilva staff, with long beard and nails, taller than any man in measure on earth.
He wandered through the worlds, divine and human, singing these verses at crossroads and in assemblies:
Who will lodge Durvasa, a brahmin honoured in his house? Hearing my declaration, who will give shelter? Whoever lodges me, let him not anger me.
No one received him, and so I lodged him.
Sometimes he ate the food of many thousands at once; sometimes he ate very little, and did not return to the house.
He would laugh suddenly and weep suddenly, and none on earth was then his equal in age.
Going to his lodging, he burned beds, bedding and adorned maidens, and then left of himself.
Then the sage of sharp vows said to me again: "Krishna, I wish to eat payasa," and he was in a hurry.
Knowing his mind, I had earlier instructed the household, "Let all kinds of food and drink, and high and low edibles, be prepared and honoured."
Then I presented the boiling payasa; having eaten it he quickly said, "Quickly smear your limbs with the payasa."
Without hesitation I did so, and I smeared my limbs and head with his leavings.
He saw your fair-faced mother nearby, and smiling he smeared her too with payasa.
The sage quickly yoked to a chariot her whose limbs were smeared with payasa, and mounting the chariot he went out of my house.
Blazing like fire, the wise brahmin, in place of a draught animal, with a goad pricked the girl Rukmini before my eyes.
And I had not even a little sorrow or jealousy then. Then he went out on the great royal road.
Seeing that great marvel, the Dasharhas, angered, spoke among themselves, speaking with one another:

Only brahmins should be born, never any other class. For who else, mounting this chariot, could live here?
mahabharata:13:144.29	The poison of a snake is sharp, but sharper still is the poison; for one burned by a brahmin-snake there is no physician.
As that invincible one went, Rukmini stumbled on the road; the glorious one could not bear it, and quickly urged her on.
Then, enraged, the brahmin leapt from the chariot and ran on foot off the road, facing south.
I ran after that best of brahmins as he ran off the road, smeared as I was with payasa: "Be gracious, blessed one."
Then, looking back, the radiant brahmin said to me: "You have conquered anger, Krishna, by your very nature, mighty-armed one.
I have seen no offence in you here, firm in vows. I am pleased with you, Govinda; choose boons as you wish. See, child, what fruit there is for me when pleased.
As long as men have affection for food, so will they have affection for you.
As long as holy fame of yours lasts in the worlds, so long you will have pre-eminence in the three worlds, and you will be very dear to all the world, Janardana.
Whatever of yours has been broken, burned or destroyed, you will see it all the same, or better, Janardana.
As long as this smearing is on your limbs, Madhusudana, you have no fear of death, as long as you wish, Achyuta.
But why was it not smeared on the soles of your feet today, my son? I do not like that." So he said to me then, pleased. So addressed, I saw my body endowed with splendour.
And, pleased, he said to Rukmini: "You will gain the best of fame among all women, and supreme glory in the world, fair one.
Neither old age nor disease nor loss of colour will touch you, lovely one; of holy fragrance, you will worship Krishna.
Among Keshava's sixteen thousand wives you will be the foremost, together with the world-honoured one, Keshava's."
Having said this to your mother, the greatly radiant Durvasa, blazing like fire, then departed and spoke again to me.
May this very mind of yours be toward brahmins, Keshava. Having said so, child, he vanished right there.
When he had vanished, I privately laid down a vow: "Whatever a brahmin says, I shall do it all."
Having kept this vow with your mother, child, I entered the house, with a joyful mind.
As soon as I entered the house, I saw everything new, whatever had been broken or burned by that brahmin, my son.
Then I was filled with wonder, seeing everything new and sound, and in my mind I honoured that twice-born, son of Rukmini.
So I then told Rukmini's son, as he asked, O bull of the Bharatas, the whole greatness of the chief of the twice-born.
So you too, son of Kunti, lord, always honour brahmins, the greatly fortunate, with words and gifts, always.
Thus I gained fortune born of the favour of brahmins, and what Bhishma here says to me is true, bull of the Bharatas.
[Yudhishthira] I wish to know in truth the greatness of that great soul and his names, O best of the wise.
[Vasudeva] Come, I shall tell you, having saluted the matted-haired god, what good I gained, great king, and what fame I won.
Hear from me, lord of the people, the Shatarudriya that I recite after rising in the morning, self-controlled and with folded hands.
Prajapati created that at the end of austerity; but Shankara created, child, creatures moving and unmoving.
There is no being higher than Mahadeva, lord of the people; in these three worlds he is the origin of beings.
No one can stand before the great soul, for no being equal to him exists in the three worlds.
Even by his smell in battle, when he is angry, enemies lose their senses, are mostly slain, tremble and fall.
Hearing his terrible roar, like the thunder of a rain cloud, the heart of the gods themselves would burst in battle.
By the sound of his bowstring all the worlds were thrown into confusion, Partha, helpless; and gods and asuras were dismayed.
The waters were churned, the earth trembled, the mountains fled, and heaven split on all sides.
The worlds, covered with blind darkness, did not shine; the light of the luminaries was lost, along with the sun, O Bharata.
Then, greatly afraid, the sages, wishing well to all beings and themselves, performed pacification and blessings.
Then, angry, of terrible valour, he rushed at the gods; enraged, he knocked out Bhaga's eyes with a blow.
With a great form he ran at Pushan and knocked out his teeth as he ate the sacrificial cake.
Then the gods, trembling, bowed to Shankara; and Rudra again fixed a blazing, sharp arrow.
Seeing Rudra's prowess, the gods with the sages, afraid, then appeased Sharva, those best of the gods.
The gods, folding their hands, recited the Shatarudriya; praised by the gods, Maheshvara was pleased.
The gods assigned Rudra a distinguished share in the sacrifice; fearful, they took refuge, O king.
By that very rage the sacrifice was mended, and whatever was destroyed there was restored in the same way.
The asuras had three strong cities in the sky, one of iron, one of silver, and another of gold.
Maghavan could not break them even with all weapons; then all the immortals, afflicted, went to Rudra for refuge.
Then the assembled great-souled gods said: "Rudra, creatures will be fierce in all their works. Kill the daityas with their cities and save the worlds, giver of honour."
So addressed, he agreed, making Vishnu the best arrow, Agni the point, Yama Vaivasvata the feathering, the Vedas the bow, and Savitri the supreme bowstring.
Having made the gods the sound of the chariot and set all in place, with a three-jointed, three-headed arrow he pierced those cities.
By an arrow bright as the sun, with the splendour of the fire of dissolution, those asuras with their cities were burned there by Rudra, O Bharata.
Seeing that child with five crests in his lap, Uma, wishing to know, then asked, "Who is this?"
Jealous, Shakra was about to strike with the thunderbolt; he stopped that arm, like an iron bar, along with the bolt.
The gods did not know him, the lord of the world; the Prajapatis were all bewildered about that Ishvara.
Then the blessed Brahma, meditating, knew "He is the best," and saluted that immeasurably mighty husband of Uma.
Then the gods appeased Uma and Rudra, and the slayer of Bala's arm became as before.
He also, becoming a brahmin named Durvasa, of great might, lived long in my house at Dvaravati.
He caused many offences in my house, and I, out of generosity, bore what was unbearable.
He is Devendra, the Wind, the Ashvins, lightning, the Moon, Ishana, the Sun and Varuna.
He is Time, the Ender, Death, darkness, night and days, fortnights, months, seasons, twilights and the year.

He is Establisher and Ordainer, Vishvakarman, all-knowing, the stars, the directions and intermediate directions, and the planets: universal form, immeasurable self, the blessed one of limitless radiance.
He is one, two, many, a hundred, a thousand, a hundred thousand.
Such is the great god, and more so; his virtues cannot be told even in hundreds of years.
They call him Fire, Mahadeva, Sthanu, Maheshvara, One-eyed, Three-eyed, Universal form and Shiva.
Brahmins who know the Veda know that god has two bodies: one terrible and the other auspicious; and those two again take many forms.
His fierce and terrible body is fire, lightning and the sun; his auspicious and gentle one is dharma, water and the moon.
Half of his self is called Fire, O best of the Bharatas; he practises celibacy, and his body is the auspicious one.
By his most terrible form he withdraws the world; because of lordship and greatness he is known as Maheshvara.
Because he burns, is sharp and fierce and mighty, eating flesh, blood and marrow, he is called Rudra.
Because he is greatest of the gods, his domain is great, and he protects the great universe, he is held to be Mahadeva.
Because he always prospers all aims by all acts, wishing welfare for men, he is held to be Shiva.
Because he protects animals in every way and delights in them, and is their lord, he is held to be Pashupati.
Because his linga stands by constant celibacy, and the worlds honour it, he is held to be Maheshvara.
One who worships the form or the linga of the great soul, worshipping the linga, always enjoys great prosperity.
Sages, gods, gandharvas and apsarases worship only that linga which stands upright.
When he is worshipped, Maheshvara rejoices; pleased, he gives happiness to devotees, fond of his devotees.
This god lives always in cremation grounds, and people sacrifice to him there, delighting in the heroes' place.
Standing unequally in bodies, he is death for creatures here, and he is wind in bodies, the prana and apana of embodied beings.
His terrible and blazing forms are many; those that are worshipped in the world, brahmins, the wise know.
His many names in the Vedas are explained truly by greatness, lordship and deeds.
In the Veda brahmins know his best Shatarudriya, and after Vyasa the praising of the great soul.
He is called giver to all worlds and the great universe; brahmins and other sages call him the eldest being.
He is the first of the gods; Fire was born from his mouth; he releases even the vital breaths stopped by many planets.
The holy-souled refuge frees those who take refuge: life, health, lordship, wealth and abundant desires.
He gives them to men, and he takes them away again; lordship over Shakra and the other gods is said to be his.
He is always greater regarding the good and bad of the three worlds; and from lordship over desires he is again called Ishvara.
He is Maheshvara of the worlds and lord of the great; by his many varied forms this world is pervaded; his mouth in the sea is the underwater fire.
[Yudhishthira] In deciding, O greatly wise one, best of the bearers of all dharma, which is the cause: direct perception or the tradition?
[Bhishma] I think there is no doubt here. Hear, wise one; you ask rightly.
Doubt is easy, O king, but decision here is hard; for what is seen and heard is endless where doubt is seen.
Reasoners who think themselves wise decide that nothing exists but what is perceived; they decide wrongly, being children who think themselves learned.
If you ask what the one cause would be, it can be found over a long time by one who is disciplined and tireless, arranging many ways of life, O Bharata.
Only by one intent on it, and no other, can this cause be reached; having reached the end of reasons, one gains vast, supreme knowledge, light for all the world.
Coming by truth, O king, and reaching the end of reasons, he is ungraspable and unbound, abandoning speech.
[Yudhishthira] Tell me, Grandsire, about perception, what is established by the world, tradition-based worlds, and the many kinds of conduct of the cultured.
Unrighteous men in the guise of dharma are like wells covered by grass; by them conduct is broken. Hear this, Yudhishthira.
Those who break it by non-conduct, bent on giving up the Veda, haters of dharma, are called fools, without doubt.
Those who are never satisfied with the good, whose minds are of the tradition, content with "this is supreme": serve them and ask them.
Those who, putting desire and wealth behind them, which follow greed and delusion, understand "this is dharma": serve them and ask them.
Their conduct is not broken by sacrifice, study and rites; conduct, cause and dharma are again the three.
[Yudhishthira] My mind is bewildered again in doubt, like one who seeks a path in the boundless and sees no far shore.
If the Vedas, perception and conduct are the authority, those three, and if they are found separate, how can dharma be one in the three?
[Bhishma] When dharma is being carried off by strong evildoers, if you think so, O king, there is three-fold inquiry into dharma.
Know it to be one; its showing is threefold. My view is that the three are separate.
The path of the three has been told; follow it so. But one should not inquire into dharma by reasoning.
Always, best of the Bharatas, let there be no doubt in you here. Like a blind, dull man without suspicion, do what I tell you.
Non-harm, truth, freedom from anger and giving: this fourfold is, Ajatashatru, the eternal dharma of one's own.
Follow the conduct among brahmins suited to father and grandfather, mighty-armed one, for they are the guides to heaven.
A foolish man who makes authority non-authority does not deserve to be an authority, for he breeds disputes.
Serve brahmins alone, honouring them and holding them in high regard; learn that all these worlds are in them.
[Bhishma] Men whose minds are overspread with passion and darkness, haters of dharma, go to hell.
But those who always attend to dharma, great king, devoted to truth and uprightness, the good, are enjoyers of heaven.
Their delight is in dharma, by serving a teacher; those who attend to dharma go to the world of the gods.
Whether men or gods, the righteous, having tormented their bodies, prosper happily, free of greed and hatred.
The wise say that dharma is Brahma's first son; the righteous attend on him as the mind on ripe fruit.
[Yudhishthira] What is the form of the unrighteous, and what do the good do? Tell me, how are the good and the bad?
[Bhishma] The ill-behaved, unassailable, foul-mouthed are the unrighteous; the good are those endowed with good conduct; that is the mark of the cultured.
The righteous do not, O king, discharge urine or faeces on the royal road, among cows, or in a cow pen.
As fire waits for its time for fuel, so a woman waits for her season; one who goes to no other woman practises celibacy; that is held so.
Nectar, brahmins and cows: these three together; therefore cows and brahmins should always be honoured by rule.
One who eats meat consecrated with the Yajus mantra is not defiled; meat from behind, meat without cause, and a son's flesh are held equal.
In his own land or another's, he should not let a guest fast; having done his work fruitfully, he should hand it over to his elders.
A seat should be given to elders; having greeted and honoured elders, they increase in life, fame and fortune.
He should never speak sharply to the aged, nor send them on errands, nor sit while they stand; so his life is not harmed.
He should not look at a naked woman, nor the wise at naked men; intercourse and food he should always keep private.
The teacher is the tirtha of tirthas, the heart the purity of the pure, supreme knowledge is the best of views, and contentment is supreme happiness.
Morning and evening he should listen to the abundant speech of the aged; a man gains learning always by serving the aged.
At study and at meals he should raise the right hand, and always restrain speech, mind and the wanderings of the senses.
Prepared payasa daily, gruel, krisara, oblation, the Ashtaka for ancestors and gods, and honouring of elders;
shaving is auspicious, greeting sneezes, and wishing long life to all the sick are proper.
Even in distress, he should never say "you" to a greater person; "you" is like an insult or killing and does not distinguish among the wise. He should behave so with inferiors, equals and pupils.
The hearts of those who do wrong always speak of sin; knowing it, they perish, hiding it from the great.
The wicked cover a deed done knowingly, saying, "Men do not see me, the gods do not see me"; the sinner, struck by sin, is born to sin.
As a usurer waits for his gain until the body breaks, so sin covered by dharma should increase dharma.
As salt dissolves when drenched in water, so sin destroyed by atonement at once perishes.
Therefore one should not hide sin; hidden, it grows. Having done it, it should be told to the good, and they pacify it.
The wealth hoarded in hope, not enjoyed in time, is taken by others at the embodied one's parting.
The wise say dharma is the mind of all beings; therefore all beings attend only to dharma.
He should practise dharma alone; he should not carry a banner of dharma; those who enjoy dharma are dealers in dharma.
He should honour the gods without pretence and serve teachers without guile; he should lay up a treasure for the next world, called giving, for the journey.
One does not get at a time of non-gain even with effort made; at a time of gain one gets vast wealth without effort; and hundreds of men are seen whose effort made bears no fruit.
If effort were the cause, a mortal would gain every fruit; and the unobtainable would not be obtained by men, best of the Bharatas.
A man who has made effort is seen without fruit, while another gains wealth by hundreds of means, and another by no means, and is happy.
Men who commit what should not be done repeatedly are seen poor, and others in unrighteousness are seen rich.
Having studied policy, one is not seen to be governed by it; why is one without knowledge taken to the ministry? The learned are unlearned, rich or poor.
If a man could gain happiness by relying on knowledge, the learned would not resort to the unlearned for a living.
As a man conquers thirst on getting water, so with knowledge one seeing the object should give up ignorance.
One does not die before his time, even pierced by hundreds of arrows; touched even by a blade of grass, one whose time has come does not live.
[Samvarta] This is true, as you say; he knows me to be a spy. Tell me one thing: where is Narada now?
Entering the house, the king, having done his forenoon rites and satisfied the best of the twice-born, then took his meal.
The last hour of this family has come, best of men; Bibhatsu will come to this city of Dvaravati.
All the sons of Dhritarashtra, rakshasas of excessive strength, rich and great-souled, purified by weapons, went to heaven; Kshatta entered Dharma, and so did King Yudhishthira.
